analysis.one_liner: Bans US public financing agencies from backing overseas oil and gas projects.
analysis.headline: The bill drew a single cosponsor, never received a hearing or a vote, and died in House committee when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop three public financing channels from funding oil and gas development overseas: the Export-Import Bank could no longer guarantee or extend credit for oil or gas projects, the Overseas Private Investment Corporation could no longer insure or finance them, and the US Treasury would have to vote against oil and gas lending at the World Bank and other multilateral development institutions. It would also require annual reports on energy-sector lending and direct the President to urge other wealthy countries to adopt the same prohibition through the OECD. Its stated aim is to redirect scarce public development money away from an industry that has ample access to private capital and toward other needs of developing countries.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, developing-country populations and the global climate would benefit from redirected public financing and fewer publicly backed fossil fuel projects, and taxpayers would stop underwriting loans and insurance for oil majors that can borrow commercially.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the Export-Import Bank from guaranteeing, insuring, or extending credit for oil or gas projects, or to any entity that would use it to finance such a project [S2][S3].
Prohibits the Overseas Private Investment Corporation from insuring, guaranteeing, or financing oil or gas projects, directly or indirectly [S2][S3].

Directs the Treasury Secretary to use the US voice and vote to oppose any assistance from multilateral development institutions to oil and gas projects, and to report annually to Congress on energy-sector lending [S2][S3].

The bill's findings note that public agencies provided more than $3 billion in financing to the international oil and gas industry in 2005, and that the World Bank's own Extractive Industries Review recommended ending oil project financing by 2008 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies would lose access to government-backed loans, guarantees, and insurance for overseas projects, and US exporters who supply equipment to those projects would lose some government-backed backing for their contracts.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil companies and their equipment exporters

drawbacks.text: Developing countries could lose a financing channel for expanding electricity and energy access, since multilateral institutions and export credit agencies have helped fund gas infrastructure in energy-poor regions; the bill itself asks for a study of whether such financing has delivered energy to impoverished populations [S3].

If US agencies withdraw, oil and gas projects could still be financed by other countries' export credit agencies with weaker environmental standards, unless other OECD members follow the US lead the bill requests [S3].
US exporters of oilfield equipment and services could lose government-backed financing that foreign competitors' governments would continue to provide.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea is straightforward: public development money is scarce and oil companies can borrow privately, so subsidizing their overseas projects with taxpayer-backed credit mainly shifts risk to the public while the emissions cost is global. The trade-off is real but narrow — some energy-poor countries might lose a financing route for power, and US exporters lose backing competitors keep — which is why a phase-down or exemptions for gas projects serving the poor is a common alternative.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees, then to a subcommittee, and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Maurice Hinchey introduced the bill on April 17, 2007, and it was referred to the Financial Services and Foreign Affairs Committees [S1][S5].
On June 8, 2007, it was referred to the Financial Services subcommittee on Domestic and International Monetary Policy, Trade, and Technology, its last recorded action [S5].
It attracted a single cosponsor, a House Democrat, and no further action occurred in the 110th Congress [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies kept their access to Export-Import Bank, OPIC, and multilateral financing, and the agencies' existing lending practices continued unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil companies and the financing agencies

for.name: Rep. Maurice Hinchey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Financial Services and Foreign Affairs Committees.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction that never considered the bill
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee in June 2007 and never brought it to a markup or floor vote in the remaining 19 months of the Congress.

against.name: Barney Frank
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee that held the bill; no hearing or markup was ever scheduled for it.

sides.party_line_note: With one sponsor and one cosponsor, both Democrats, no opposition is recorded in the action history, so no partisan split ever materialized.

industries.note: The bill would cut off Export-Import Bank, OPIC, and multilateral financing for their overseas projects. Public backing shifts project risk to taxpayers for an industry with $1.6 trillion in 2005 revenues and broad access to private capital markets [S3].

industries.industry: Export credit and project finance markets (banks and insurers around Ex-Im and OPIC)
industries.note: The bill removes a slice of publicly guaranteed oil and gas deal flow that private banks and insurers currently win alongside Ex-Im and OPIC. The public bears the risk when those guarantees are used.

industries.industry: US exporters of oilfield equipment and services
industries.note: These suppliers rely on Ex-Im guarantees to compete for contracts on overseas oil and gas projects, and they would lose that backing while foreign competitors keep theirs.
